passages.happening:
The chapter opens with a date. ‘In the four hundred and eightieth year after the Israelites had come out of the land of Egypt’, in the month of Ziv, in the fourth year of his reign, Solomon begins to build the house of the LORD (verse 1).

“The house that King Solomon built for the LORD was sixty cubits long, twenty cubits wide, and thirty cubits high” (verse 2). A porch runs across its front. There are narrow windows high in the walls, and around the outside a building of side rooms rises three floors, each a little wider than the one below (verses 3-6).

“The temple was constructed using finished stones cut at the quarry, so that no hammer or chisel or any other iron tool was heard in the temple while it was being built” (verse 7). Solomon builds it and roofs it with beams and planks of cedar (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
This is the moment the Bible has been moving toward since the exodus. At Sinai God gave instructions for a portable sanctuary, the tabernacle, so that he could live among his people as they traveled. Now, with Israel settled and at rest, the tent gives way to a permanent house in the city God chose. The date in verse 1 ties the temple to the exodus, as if to say that the rescue from Egypt reaches its goal here.

A cubit was about eighteen inches, so the main building was about ninety feet long, thirty feet wide and forty-five feet high. That is not large by modern standards, but it was richly finished. Its plan, a porch, a main hall and an inner room in a row, closely resembles Iron Age temples found elsewhere in the region, especially at Ain Dara in northern Syria and at Tell Tayinat in southern Turkey. No remains of Solomon's temple have been excavated, since the Temple Mount is not open to digging and later building covers it.

Ziv fell in spring, roughly April to May. It is an old Canaanite month name, which the narrator explains as the second month.

The quiet of the building site recalls the law that an altar was not to be built of stones shaped with tools. The holy place was kept set apart even while it rose.
passages.later: At Sinai God had said, “And they are to make a sanctuary for Me, so that I may dwell among them” (Exodus 25:8). And the law for altars said, ‘you must not build it with stones shaped by tools’ (Exodus 20:25).
passages.hard:
Does the 480 years of verse 1 settle the date of the exodus?

It is one of the main pieces of evidence, and it is read in more than one way. Those who hold the early date, about 1446 BC, take the number as a count of years, and point to other texts that seem to agree with it, such as Judges 11:26. Those who hold a later date, in the thirteenth century BC, point to historical and archaeological considerations, among them the city named Rameses in Exodus 1:11. They suggest that 480 is a round figure built from twelve generations of forty years, forty being a common biblical number for a generation, when a real generation was often nearer twenty-five years.

Both positions are held by scholars who take the Bible's history seriously, and the site's page on the exodus sets out the evidence. What the verse plainly does is tie the temple to the exodus, and present it as the goal of God's rescue of Israel from Egypt.
passages.asks: Solomon dated the work from the exodus, as if everything since had been leading there. Ask what in your own life you date from the time God set you free. And ask what holy work in your life needs quiet, without the noise of hammers.

passages.t: A word in the middle of the building
passages.happening:
In the middle of the work, ‘the word of the LORD came to Solomon’ (verse 11): “As for this temple you are building, if you walk in My statutes, carry out My ordinances, and keep all My commandments by walking in them, I will fulfill through you the promise I made to your father David” (verse 12).

“And I will dwell among the Israelites and will not abandon My people Israel” (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
These three verses sit right in the middle of the building report and interrupt it, so that the reader cannot miss the point. The house matters only if God lives there, and his living there is tied to faithfulness, not to cedar and gold.

The verb for dwell, shakan, is the root of mishkan, the word for the tabernacle, and later Jewish tradition used shekinah for God's dwelling presence. It speaks of God making his home among his people. The verb for abandon is the one used when Israel forsakes the LORD, and the book of Kings will show God's patience tested again and again by that forsaking.

The temple stood for nearly four hundred years, until Babylon destroyed it in 587 or 586 BC. The first readers of Kings read this promise knowing that the building was gone. The chapter told them that God's presence had never depended on the building.
passages.later: God had made the same promise at Sinai: “Then I will dwell among the Israelites and be their God” (Exodus 29:45).
passages.asks: God interrupted the building to speak about obedience. Ask what you are building for God that he might interrupt to ask about your heart. And ask whether you are trusting the work to keep God near, or trusting God.

passages.t: Cedar, gold, and the inner room
passages.happening:
Solomon lines the inside of the house with cedar from floor to ceiling and covers the floor with cypress (verse 15). At the back he walls off twenty cubits with cedar boards to make an inner room, ‘the Most Holy Place’ (verse 16). The main hall in front of it is forty cubits long (verse 17). The cedar is carved with gourds and open flowers: ‘Everything was cedar; not a stone could be seen’ (verse 18).

The inner room is made ready for the ark of the covenant (verse 19). “The inner sanctuary was twenty cubits long, twenty cubits wide, and twenty cubits high” (verse 20). Solomon overlays it, and the whole inside of the temple, with pure gold (verses 20-22).

In the inner room he sets two cherubim of olive wood, each ten cubits high, with wings ten cubits across. Their outer wings touch the two walls, and their inner wings touch each other in the middle of the room (verses 23-27). He overlays them with gold (verse 28).
passages.hearers:
An ancient temple was a god's house, not a meeting hall. Ordinary Israelites gathered in the courts, where the altar of sacrifice stood. Only priests entered the main hall, and only the high priest entered the inner room, once a year. The building was arranged in zones of growing holiness, from court to hall to inner room, following the pattern of the tabernacle.

The inner room, in Hebrew devir, is a perfect cube, twenty cubits each way. Its shape expresses completeness and holiness. It is the heart of Israel's worship.

Cherubim were winged guardian figures of God's throne and presence. The ark itself was topped with two small ones. Here two great ones, about fifteen feet tall, spread their wings over the place where the ark will stand, a picture of God's heavenly throne. They are not the chubby infants of later art.

Temples around Israel held a statue of their god in the inner room. Israel's held none. The God enthroned above the cherubim could not be pictured.
passages.later:
The ark's own cherubim are described in Exodus: ‘And the cherubim are to have wings that spread upward, overshadowing the mercy seat’ (Exodus 25:20). The law allowed the inner room to be entered for atonement ‘once a year for the Israelites because of all their sins’ (Leviticus 16:34).

John saw the new Jerusalem laid out in the same shape: ‘The city lies foursquare, with its width the same as its length’ (Revelation 21:16).
passages.asks: Everything inside was cedar and gold, and not a stone could be seen. Ask what the care Solomon took over God's house says about the reverence God deserves. And ask whether you come to God lightly, as if he were easy to come near.

passages.happening:
The walls all around, in the inner and outer rooms, are carved with cherubim, palm trees and open flowers, and the floor is overlaid with gold (verses 29-30). The doors of the inner room are of olive wood, carved with cherubim, palm trees and flowers, and covered with hammered gold (verses 31-32). The doors of the main hall are of cypress, each with two folding panels, carved and gilded the same way (verses 33-35). An inner courtyard is built with three rows of dressed stone and a row of cedar beams (verse 36).

The foundation was laid in Solomon's fourth year, in the month of Ziv. “In his eleventh year and eighth month, the month of Bul, the temple was finished in every detail and according to every specification. So he built the temple in seven years” (verse 38).
passages.hearers:
The decoration carried meaning. Palm trees, gourds and open flowers, carved everywhere and covered with gold, made the inside a kind of garden. Many interpreters see an echo of Eden, where cherubim guarded the way to the tree of life after the first man and woman were sent out. The temple was a place where the presence of God, lost in the garden, could be approached again.

The chapter reads like a builder's record, moving from the outside in, then to the carvings and the doors. The phrase that Solomon built the temple and finished it comes in verses 9 and 14, and the last verse closes the account: finished in every detail.

Bul fell in autumn, roughly October to November. Like Ziv, it is an old Canaanite month name.
passages.later: Genesis tells why cherubim guard a garden: “So He drove out the man and stationed cherubim on the east side of the Garden of Eden, along with a whirling sword of flame to guard the way to the tree of life” (Genesis 3:24).
passages.asks: Solomon carved a garden in gold in a house where God could be approached again. Ask what it means to you that God wants to be near his people. And ask what you have finished, and what you have left half-built, in the work God has given you.
